claim: Astrocytes regulate the formation and function of neuronal synapses via multiple signals.
source: Astrocytes regulate the formation and function of neuronal synapses via multiple signals; however, what controls regional and temporal expression of these signals during development is unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Astrocyte synapse-regulating genes show differential temporal and layer-enriched expression in the developing mouse visual cortex.
source: We determined the expression profile of astrocyte synapse-regulating genes in the developing mouse visual cortex, identifying astrocyte signals that show differential temporal and layer-enriched expression.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by RNA sequencing and in situ hybridization data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The temporal and layer-enriched expression patterns of astrocyte synapse-regulating genes are not intrinsic to astrocytes.
source: These patterns are not intrinsic to astrocytes, but regulated by visually evoked neuronal activity, as they are absent in mice lacking glutamate release from thalamocortical terminals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments using VGlut2 conditional knockout mice showing altered gene expression patterns.

claim: Synapses remain immature in mice lacking glutamate release from thalamocortical terminals.
source: These patterns are not intrinsic to astrocytes, but regulated by visually evoked neuronal activity, as they are absent in mice lacking glutamate release from thalamocortical terminals. Consequently, synapses remain immature.
evidence: This is supported by data showing altered GLUA1 and GLUA2 levels in VGlut2 cKO mice.

claim: Expression of synapse-regulating genes and synaptic development is altered when astrocyte signaling is blunted by diminishing calcium release from astrocyte stores.
source: Expression of synapse-regulating genes and synaptic development is also altered when astrocyte signaling is blunted by diminishing calcium release from astrocyte stores.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using Ip3r2 KO mice showing changes in gene expression and synaptic protein levels.

claim: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing identified groups of astrocytic genes regulated by neuronal and astrocyte activity.
source: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing identified groups of astrocytic genes regulated by neuronal and astrocyte activity, and a cassette of genes that show layer-specific enrichment.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the snRNAseq experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The development of cortical circuits requires coordinated signaling between astrocytes and neurons.
source: Thus, the development of cortical circuits requires coordinated signaling between astrocytes and neurons, highlighting astrocytes as a target to manipulate in neurodevelopmental disorders.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing interdependence of neuronal and astrocyte activity in circuit development.

claim: Synapse development in the rodent cortex occurs over the first postnatal month, initiating at around postnatal day (P) 7, peaking at P14, and stabilizing towards P28.
source: In the rodent cortex, this occurs over the period of the first postnatal month, initiating at around postnatal day (P) 7, peaking at P14, and stabilizing towards P28 (Blue and Parnavelas, 1983a; Blue and Parnavelas, 1983b; Farhy-Tselnicker and Allen, 2018; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Synaptic deficits caused by mutations in synapse-related genes are associated with developmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and epilepsy.
source: Synaptic deficits, for example, caused by mutations in synapse-related genes, are associated with developmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder and epilepsy (Lepeta et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The majority of synapses in the mammalian cortex are contacted by astrocytes.
source: The majority of synapses in the mammalian cortex are contacted by astrocytes, a type of glia and key regulators of circuit development and function (Allen, 2013; Batool et al., 2019; Bernardinelli et al., 2014a; Genoud et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Thrombospondin family members induce formation of structurally normal but functionally silent synapses.
source: For example, thrombospondin family members induce formation of structurally normal but functionally silent synapses (Christopherson et al., 2005; Eroglu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Glypicans induce the formation of active synapses by recruiting GLUA1 to the postsynaptic side.
source: Glypicans induce the formation of active synapses by recruiting GLUA1 to the postsynaptic side (Allen et al., 2012; Farhy-Tselnicker et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Chordin-like 1 induces synapse maturation by recruiting GLUA2 to the postsynaptic side.
source: chordin-like 1 induces synapse maturation by recruiting GLUA2 to the postsynaptic side (Blanco-Suarez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Before eye opening (from birth to ~P12 in mice), spontaneous retinal activity evokes correlated cortical responses.
source: Before eye opening (from birth to ~P12 in mice), spontaneous retinal activity evokes correlated cortical responses (Gribizis et al., 2019; Hanganu et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Spontaneous retinal activity is important for the correct establishment of thalamocortical synapses.
source: spontaneous retinal activity evokes correlated cortical responses (Gribizis et al., 2019; Hanganu et al., 2006) that are important for the correct establishment of thalamocortical synapses (Cang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Eye opening marks a step towards synapse maturation in the visual cortex, with the appearance of visually evoked neuronal responses.
source: Eye opening marks a step towards synapse maturation in the VC, with the appearance of visually evoked neuronal responses across the retinal-LGN-VC circuit (Espinosa and Stryker, 2012; Hooks and Chen, 2006; Hooks and Chen, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Visual deprivation methods such as dark rearing delay both synaptic and astrocyte maturation.
source: Perturbing this process by methods of visual deprivation, such as dark rearing, delays both synaptic (Albanese et al., 1983; Desai et al., 2002; Freire, 1978; Funahashi et al., 2013; Hsu et al., 2018; Ishikawa et al., 2014; Ko et al., 2014; Majdan and Shatz, 2006; Tropea et al., 2006) and astrocyte maturation (Müller, 1990; Stogsdill et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cortical astrocytes are spatially arranged in diverse populations.
source: Recent work has shown that cortical astrocytes are also spatially arranged in diverse populations (Batiuk et al., 2020; Bayraktar et al., 2020; John Lin et al., 2017; Lanjakornsiripan et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Astrocyte heterogeneity has been observed in multiple brain regions.
source: in line with evidence from other brain regions showing astrocyte heterogeneity (Chaboub and Deneen, 2012; Chai et al., 2017; Khakh and Deneen, 2019; Oberheim et al., 2012; Rusnakova et al., 2013; Schitine et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is a significant enrichment in astrocytic genes over other cell types in the mRNA isolated by HA immunopurification compared to total visual cortex mRNA.
source: We found a significant enrichment in astrocytic genes over other cell types in the mRNA isolated by HA immunopurification (IP; labeled Astro) compared to total VC mRNA (input; IN; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: More than 95% of S100β-positive cells are also positive for the HA tag in the visual cortex at P28.
source: Furthermore, immunostaining analysis of VC sections at P28 shows a high overlap between the HA ribosome tag and the astrocyte marker S100β, but not with other cell-type markers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D), with more than 95% of S100β-positive cells also positive for the HA tag
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Principal component analysis shows P7 and P14 astrocyte samples clustering separately from other ages, while P28 and P120 samples cluster together.
source: This showed that P7 and P14 astrocytes form distinct clusters, while P28 and P120 astrocytes cluster together.
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The largest number of differentially expressed genes in astrocytes is between P7 and P28 (~6000 total genes).
source: The largest number of DEGs is between P7 and P28 (~6000 total genes), and smallest numbers between P14 and P28 (~1000 total genes), and P28 and P120 (~2000 total genes).
evidence: This is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Approximately 60% of all astrocyte-enriched genes are significantly changed from P7 to P14.
source: Analysis of astrocyte-enriched genes (IP/input > 3) showed that ~60% of all astrocyte-enriched genes are significantly changed from P7 to P14, while only ~20% are changing between P28 and P120 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Genes common to all ages in astrocytes are enriched in GO terms related to cholesterol processing and serine synthesis.
source: This showed that genes common to all ages are enriched in GO terms related to cholesterol processing and serine synthesis, confirming the previously established important role of astrocytes in regulating brain cholesterol (Orth and Bellosta, 2012; Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 1G and cited literature.

claim: At P7, astrocyte genes are enriched in GO terms related to cortical development.
source: Analysis of GO terms unique to each age showed that at P7 astrocyte genes are enriched in GO terms related to cortical development
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: At P14, astrocyte genes are enriched in GO terms related to Wnt and BMP signaling pathways.
source: while at P14 astrocyte genes are enriched in GO terms related to Wnt and BMP signaling pathways.
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Adult astrocytes (P120) are enriched in GO terms related to regulation of extracellular matrix assembly and contact inhibition.
source: Conversely, adult astrocytes (P120) are enriched in terms related to regulation of extracellular matrix assembly and contact inhibition (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Apoe and Cst3 are the most highly expressed genes in astrocytes at all ages (peak FPKM ~10,000).
source: We found that Apoe and Cst3 are the most highly expressed genes in astrocytes at all ages (peak FPKM ~10,000; Figure 1F, Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Lars2 is the most astrocyte-enriched gene at all ages amongst highly expressed astrocyte genes (FPKM >100) with astro IP/input ~40.
source: while amongst highly expressed astrocyte genes (FPKM >100) Lars2 is the most astrocyte-enriched gene at all ages (astro IP/ input ~40; Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Aldh1l1 expression is stable across all ages in astrocytes.
source: The expression of another well-known astrocytic gene Aldh1l1 (Morel et al., 2017; Figure 1I) is stable across all ages, making it an optimal marker for astrocytes during both development and in the adult (Srinivasan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1I and cited literature.

claim: S100b expression is upregulated later in development, making it more suitable to mark adult astrocytes.
source: On the other hand, S100b expression is upregulated later in development, making it more suitable to mark adult astrocytes (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The metabotropic glutamate receptor Grm5 (mGluR5) is most highly expressed at P7 and then declines with maturation.
source: For genes that encode proteins important for astrocyte function, we found that the metabotropic glutamate receptor Grm5 (mGluR5) is most highly expressed at P7 and then declines with maturation, confirming previous reports (Catania et al., 1994; Sun et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1I and cited literature.

claim: The glutamate transporter Slc1a2 (Glt1) and the connexins (Gja1, Gjb6) are significantly upregulated from P14 onwards.
source: while the glutamate transporter Slc1a2 (Glt1) and the connexins (Gja1, Gjb6) are significantly upregulated from P14 onwards (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Thbs1 is significantly higher at P7 than later ages.
source: The family members expressed by astrocytes in the CNS show divergent expression, with Thbs1 being significantly higher at P7 than later ages
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Thbs4 is significantly higher at P120 than P7.
source: whereas Thbs4 is significantly higher at P120 than P7 (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Gpc4 is most highly expressed at P7 and gradually declines with maturation.
source: Gpc4 and Gpc6 show different temporal expression in vivo. While Gpc4 is most highly expressed at P7 and gradually declines with maturation
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Gpc6 peaks at P14–P28.
source: Gpc6 peaks at P14–P28.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Gpc5 has low expression at P7 and is significantly increased at all later ages.
source: Gpc5, a glypican family member with yet unknown function, has low expression at P7, and is significantly increased at all later ages.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Chrdl1 expression peaks at P14.
source: Astrocyte-secreted chordin-like 1 (Chrdl1) regulates synapse maturation and its expression peaks at P14, confirming previous analysis (Blanco-Suarez et al., 2018; Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1J and cited literature.

claim: Astrocyte phagocytic receptors Megf10 and Mertk significantly increase in expression between P7 and P14.
source: Astrocyte phagocytic receptors involved in synapse elimination, Megf10 and Mertk (Chung et al., 2013), significantly increase in expression between P7 and P14, coincident with the initiation of synapse elimination.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1J and cited literature.

claim: At birth (P1), very few astrocytes are present in the visual cortex, comprising 0.5–2% of the total cell number.
source: At birth (P1), very few astrocytes are present, comprising 0.5–2% of the total cell number in the VC (represented as GFP-positive cells as a percentage of all cells marked by the nuclear dye DAPI)
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: At P1, there is a significantly higher percentage of astrocytes in deeper layers than upper layers of the visual cortex.
source: with a significantly higher percentage of astrocytes in deeper layers than upper layers (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—source data 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The astrocyte percentage increases with development in all cortical layers, peaking at P21–P28.
source: The astrocyte percentage increases with development in all cortical layers, peaking at P21–P28.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: At P21-P28, astrocytes are ~10% of total cell number in layers 2–6, and ~50% in L1.
source: At this time, astrocytes are ~10% of total cell number in layers (L) 2–6, and ~50% in L1 (Figure 2C and D, Figure 2—source data 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: There is a significant decrease in DAPI-positive nuclei per mm2 of visual cortex from P1 to P14–P28.
source: As the brain develops, the distance between cells grows to accommodate the increase in cell size and complexity, as evident by a significant decrease in DAPI-positive nuclei per mm2 of VC that occurs from P1 to P14–P28 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2—source data 1A).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The proportion of astrocytes remains constant in all cortical layers and across ages, with the exception of L1–2/3, where it is significantly lower at P1.
source: Despite this decrease in total cell density, the proportion of astrocytes remains constant in all cortical layers and across ages, with the exception of L1–2/3, where it is significantly lower at P1 (Figure 2C and E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C and E.

claim: Gpc4 expression decreases between P7 and P14 only in L1 astrocytes, staying stable across development in all other layers.
source: Layer-specific analysis, however, shows that these differences are driven by astrocytes in L1: Gpc4 expression decreases between P7 and P14 only in L1 astrocytes, staying stable across development in all other layers (thresh area [μm2] L1: P4 3.1 ± 0.5; P7 4.1 ± 0.1; P14 1.7 ± 0.2; P28 1.1 ± 0.3; Figure 2F and G, Figure 2—source data 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Gpc6 expression increases in astrocytes between P7 and P14 in L2–5, with significant upregulation in L5, and remains high at P28.
source: Layer-specific analysis showed that this increase occurs in astrocytes between P7 and P14 in L2–5, with significant upregulation in L5, and remaining high at P28 (thresh area [μm2] L5: P4 2.5 ± 0.4; P7 2.5 ± 0.4; P14 4.4 ± 0.4; P28 3.1 ± 0.4; Figure 2H and I, Figure 2—source data 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 2H and I.

claim: Gpc5 is strongly upregulated at P14 and remains high at P28 in astrocytes in all layers.
source: Gpc5 is strongly upregulated at P14 and remains high at P28 in astrocytes in all layers, matching the bulk RNAseq data (thresh area [μm2] L1: P4 0.5 ± 0.1; P7 1.3 ± 0.2; P14 5.9 ± 0.7; P28 5.3 ± 1.1; Figure 2J and K, Figure 2—source data 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 2J and K.

claim: Chrdl1 expression increases from P7 to P14 in a layer-specific manner, with the largest increase in upper layer astrocytes and significant upregulation in L2/3.
source: Spatial analysis revealed that this increase from P7 to P14 is layer-specific, with the largest increase in Chrdl1 occurring in upper layer astrocytes with significant upregulation in L2/3 (thresh area [μm2] L2/3: P4 4.1 ± 0.2; P7 4.1 ± 1; P14 9.9 ± 0.6; P28 7.6 ± 1; Figure 2L and M, Figure 2—source data 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 2L and M.

claim: At its peak of expression, Chrdl1 is highest in L1–4 astrocytes compared to L5–6.
source: Further, at its peak of expression, Chrdl1 is highest in L1–4 astrocytes compared to L5–6, demonstrating a heterogeneous expression across layers, as previously reported (Bayraktar et al., 2020; Blanco-Suarez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 2L and M and cited literature.

claim: Thbs2 expression increases in L4–5 at P28.
source: Nevertheless, we observed an increase in Thbs2 expression in L4–5 at P28 (thresh area [μm2] L5: P4 0.7 ± 0.1; P7 0.7 ± 0.19; P14 1 ± 0.1; P28 1.8 ± 0.3; Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and E, Figure 2—source data 1B)
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: Thbs4 expression increases at P28 in all layers.
source: and an increase in Thbs4 at P28 in all layers (thresh area [μm2] L1: P4 0.1 ± 0.01; P7 0.1 ± 0.1; P14 0.3 ± 0.1; P28 1.9 ± 0.5; Figure 2—figure supplement 2F and G, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F and G.

claim: GLUA1 levels peak at earlier time points than GLUA2.
source: As expected based on the literature, GLUA1 levels peak at earlier time points than GLUA2 (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3C and D and cited literature.

claim: GLUA2 immunoreactivity significantly increases from P7 to P14 in L1–5, and then remains stable to P28.
source: GLUA2 immunoreactivity significantly increases from P7 to P14 in L1–5, and then remains stable to P28 (Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: At all ages, the levels of GLUA1 and GLUA2 are significantly higher in L1 than all other layers.
source: At all ages, the levels of GLUA1 and GLUA2 are significantly higher in L1 than all other layers, consistent with L1 being rich in synaptic connections (Figure 3—source data 1; Douglas and Martin, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3 and cited literature.

claim: VGLUT1 immunoreactivity greatly increases between P7 and P14 in all cortical layers and remains stable at later ages.
source: VGLUT1 immunoreactivity greatly increases between P7 and P14 in all cortical layers and remains stable at later ages (Figure 3G and H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: VGLUT2 levels steadily increase from P1 to P14, and then remain stable.
source: VGLUT2 levels steadily increase from P1 to P14, and then remain stable.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3I and J.

claim: VGLUT2 immunoreactivity is significantly higher in L1 and L4 than other layers at all ages.
source: VGLUT2 immunoreactivity is significantly higher in L1 and L4 than other layers at all ages, consistent with these being thalamic innervation zones and previous findings in rat cortex (Figure 3I and J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—source data 1; Boulland et al., 2004; Conti et al., 2005; Fremeau et al., 2001; Lopez-Bendito and Molnar, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3I and J and cited literature.

claim: GPC4 protein secretion from astrocytes is significantly reduced in the presence of neurons.
source: Our experiments using cultured astrocytes and neurons show that GPC4 protein secretion from astrocytes is significantly reduced in the presence of neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1)
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GPC4 protein secretion from astrocytes is significantly reduced when astrocytes are incubated with neurotransmitters including glutamate, adenosine, or ATP.
source: or when astrocytes are incubated with neurotransmitters including glutamate, adenosine, or ATP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is a significant decrease in VGLUT2 signal in the visual cortex of VGlut2 cKO mice compared to WT at P14.
source: Immunostaining experiments showed a significant decrease in VGLUT2 signal in the VC of VGlut2 cKO mice compared to WT at P14 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: VGlut2 cKO did not strongly affect the levels of VGLUT1, which marks cortico-cortical connections.
source: Notably, VGlut2 cKO did not strongly affect the levels of VGLUT1, which marks cortico-cortical connections (Figure 4C; Wallén-Mackenzie et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C and cited literature.

claim: A small but significant increase in VGLUT1 immunoreactivity was observed in L4 in VGlut2 cKO mice.
source: though a small but significant increase in VGLUT1 immunoreactivity was observed in L4, a major target of thalamocortical projections.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: VGlut2 WT and cKO mice show a comparable number and volume of tdTomato-labeled projections in L1 and L4 of the visual cortex.
source: All cre+ tdTomato+ groups (VGlut2 WT (Slc17a6+/+), VGlut2 cHet (Slc17a6f/+), and VGlut2 cKO (Slc17a6f/f)) showed a comparable number and volume of tdTomato-labeled projections in L1 and L4 of the VC (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: VGLUT2 puncta colocalized with tdTomato-positive axons show a significant decrease in number in VGlut2 cHet and VGlut2 cKO compared to WT.
source: Analysis of VGLUT2 puncta colocalized with tdTomato-positive axons showed a significant decrease in number in VGlut2 cHet and VGlut2 cKO compared to WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and C.

claim: The number of cortical astrocytes marked by Slc1a3 is not affected by VGlut2 cKO in any cortical layer at P14.
source: The number of cortical astrocytes marked by Slc1a3, and the expression level of Slc1a3 mRNA, is not affected by VGlut2 cKO in any cortical layer at P14, showing that gross astrocyte development proceeds normally in the absence of thalamic input (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D and E.

claim: Gpc4 expression is significantly increased in VGlut2 cKO compared to WT at P14 specifically in L1 astrocytes and unchanged in all other layers.
source: In VGlut2 cKO mice, this change no longer occurs (Figure 4D and E). Gpc4 expression is significantly increased in VGlut2 cKO compared to WT at P14 specifically in L1 astrocytes and unchanged in all other layers (thresh area [μm2]: L1 WT 1.3 ± 0.1; cKO 2.3 ± 0.2; Figure 4D and E, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Gpc6 is lower in astrocytes in layers 4 and 5 in VGlut2 cKO than in the WT at P14.
source: In the absence of thalamic glutamate release, Gpc6 is lower in astrocytes in layers 4 and 5 than in the WT at P14, showing that the normal developmental upregulation has been blocked (thresh area [μm2]: L4 WT 2.7 ± 0.4; cKO 1.5 ± 0.1; Figure 4F and G, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Chrdl1 expression is significantly decreased in VGlut2 cKO compared to WT specifically in astrocytes in upper layers (1–4), and not affected in deep layers at P14.
source: Similarly, Chrdl1 expression normally increases in upper layer astrocytes between P7 and P14 (Figure 2L and M); however, it is significantly decreased in VGlut2 cKO compared to WT specifically in astrocytes in upper layers (1–4), and not affected in deep layers at P14 (thresh area [μm2]: L1 WT 6 ± 0.4; cKO 4.6 ± 0.5; Figure 4H and I, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 4H and I.

claim: At P7, there is no difference in expression of Gpc4, Gpc6, or Chrdl1 between VGlut2 cKO and WT mice.
source: To determine if these alterations are due to the loss of thalamic neuron glutamate release at a specific developmental time (e.g., eye opening at ~P12), we analyzed the expression of Gpc4, Gpc6, and Chrdl1 at P7 (prior to eye opening). We found no difference in expression of any of these genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2H–J)
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2H–J.

claim: There is no change in VGLUT1 puncta in the absence of VGLUT2 in VGlut2 cKO mice at P14.
source: We first analyzed cortico-cortical synapses marked by VGLUT1 and found that, as in the low-resolution characterization (Figure 4C), there is no change in VGLUT1 puncta in the absence of VGLUT2 (Figure 4J, K, N and O).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4J, K, N and O.

claim: There is a significant increase in the number of GLUA1 puncta and their colocalization with VGLUT1 in the VGlut2 cKO in L1 at P14.
source: In the case of GLUA1 containing AMPARs, which are regulated by Gpc4, we found a significant increase in the number of GLUA1 puncta and their colocalization with VGLUT1 in the VGlut2 cKO, correlating with the observed increase in Gpc4 (GLUA1 FC 1.24 ± 0.04; Figure 4J and L; Coloc FC 1.38 ± 0.07; Figure 4J and M).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4J, L, and M.

claim: There is a significant decrease in both the number of GLUA2 puncta and the number of colocalized GLUA2-VGLUT1 puncta in VGlut2 cKO mice compared to WT in L1 at P14.
source: For GLUA2 containing AMPARs, which are regulated by Chrdl1, we found a significant decrease in both the number of GLUA2 puncta and the number of colocalized GLUA2-VGLUT1 puncta in VGlut2 cKO mice compared to WT, correlating with the observed decrease in Chrdl1 (GLUA2 FC 0.77 ± 0.04; Figure 4N and P; Coloc FC 0.75 ± 0.1; Figure 4N and Q).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4N, P, and Q.

claim: There is no difference in the number of Bassoon puncta colocalized with tdTomato between the WT and cKO mice at thalamocortical synapses.
source: We found no difference in the number of Bassoon puncta colocalized with tdTomato between the WT and cKO mice, a further indication that synapses form in the absence of VGLUT2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2K, L, O, P), and fitting with findings from mice that globally lack presynaptic release (Verhage et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2K, L, O, P and cited literature.

claim: There is an increase in GLUA1 and colocalization of GLUA1 with Bassoon and tdTomato at thalamocortical synapses in VGlut2 cKO mice.
source: As is the case for cortico-cortical synapses, we found an increase in GLUA1 and colocalization of GLUA1 with Bassoon and tdTomato (GLUA1 FC 1.21 ± 0.09; Figure 4—figure supplement 2K and M; Coloc FC 1.36 ± 0.23; Figure 4—figure supplement 2K and N)
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2K, M, and N.

claim: There is a decrease in total GLUA2 and GLUA2-Bassoon synapses at thalamocortical synapses in VGlut2 cKO mice.
source: and a decrease in total GLUA2 and GLUA2-Bassoon synapses (GLUA2 FC 0.70 ± 0.08; Figure 4—figure supplement 2O and Q; Coloc FC 0.65 ± 0.13; Figure 4—figure supplement 2O and R).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2O, Q, and R.

claim: Knocking out Ip3r2 does not affect the number of astrocytes or the expression levels of Slc1a3 at P14.
source: At P14, knocking out Ip3r2 does not affect the number of astrocytes or the expression levels of Slc1a3, showing astrocytes develop grossly normally when store-mediated calcium release is diminished (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B, Figure 5—source data 1, Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Gpc4 mRNA level is reduced in astrocytes in all layers in Ip3r2 KO mice, with a significant decrease occurring in L1, 4, and 6 at P14.
source: In the case of Gpc4, the mRNA level is reduced in astrocytes in all layers, with a significant decrease occurring in L1, 4, and 6 (thresh area [μm2]: L1 WT 1.5 ± 0.1; KO 1.1 ± 0.1; Figure 5C and D, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: There is no difference in Gpc6 mRNA level between Ip3r2 KO and WT in astrocytes in any layer at P14.
source: For Gpc6, there is no difference in the mRNA level between Ip3r2 KO and WT in astrocytes in any layer (Figure 5E and F, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Chrdl1 expression is increased in astrocytes in all layers in Ip3r2 KO mice, with a significant increase occurring in L1, 2/3, and 5 at P14.
source: Chrdl1 expression is increased in astrocytes in all layers, with a significant increase occurring in L1, 2/3, and 5 (thresh area [μm2]: L1 WT 7.3 ± 1.1; KO 10.6 ± 1; Figure 5G and H, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: At P7, there is no change in astrocyte number or Slc1a3 mRNA signal in Ip3r2 KO mice.
source: As with P14, at P7 there is no change in astrocyte number or Slc1a3 mRNA signal, showing astrocytes develop grossly normally (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: At P7, there is no difference in expression of Gpc4 and Chrdl1 between Ip3r2 KO and WT.
source: In the case of Gpc4 and Chrdl1, there is no difference in expression between Ip3r2 KO and WT at P7 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and G)
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E and G.

claim: At P7, there is a significant increase in Gpc6 expression in the Ip3r2 KO restricted to L4.
source: whereas for Gpc6 there is a significant increase in the Ip3r2 KO restricted to L4 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The numbers of both cortico-cortical presynaptic terminals marked by VGLUT1, and thalamocortical terminals marked by VGLUT2, are significantly decreased in Ip3r2 KO mice compared to WT in L1 at P14.
source: We found that the numbers of both cortico-cortical presynaptic terminals marked by VGLUT1, and thalamocortical terminals marked by VGLUT2, are significantly decreased in Ip3r2 KO mice compared to WT, demonstrating a global deficit in synapse formation in the absence of astrocyte calcium signaling (VGLUT1 from GLUA1: FC 0.86 ± 0.04; Figure 5I and J; VGLUT1 from GLUA2: FC 0.87 ± 0.05; Figure 5M and N. VGLUT2 from GLUA1: FC 0.89 ± 0.05; Figure 5—figure supplement 1H and I; VGLUT2 from GLUA2: FC 0.80 ± 0.05; Figure 5—figure supplement 1L and M).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5I, J, M, N and Figure 5—figure supplement 1H, I, L, M.

claim: There is a significant decrease in the total number of GLUA1 puncta and their colocalization with VGLUT1 and VGLUT2 in the Ip3r2 KO in L1 at P14.
source: For GLUA1 containing AMPARs, which are regulated by Gpc4, we found a significant decrease in the total number of puncta and their colocalization with VGLUT1 and VGLUT2 in the Ip3r2 KO, correlating with the observed decrease in Gpc4 mRNA (VGLUT1-GLUA1: GLUA1 FC 0.84 ± 0.03; Figure 5I and K; Coloc FC 0.70 ± 0.03; Figure 5I and L; VGLUT2-GLUA1: GLUA1 FC 0.83 ± 0.03; Figure 5—figure supplement 1H and J; Coloc FC 0.74 ± 0.03; Figure 5—figure supplement 1H and K).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5I, K, L and Figure 5—figure supplement 1H, J, K.

claim: There is a significant increase in GLUA2 puncta number in Ip3r2 KO mice in L1 at P14.
source: For GLUA2 containing AMPARs, which are regulated by Chrdl1, we found a significant increase in their number, correlating with the observed increase in Chrdl1 (VGLUT1-GLUA2: GLUA2 FC 1.22 ± 0.07; Figure 5M and O; VGLUT2-GLUA2: GLUA2 FC 1.14 ± 0.03; Figure 5—figure supplement 1L and N).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5M, O and Figure 5—figure supplement 1L, N.

claim: The number of colocalized presynaptic puncta and GLUA2 is unchanged in Ip3r2 KO mice in L1 at P14.
source: The number of colocalized presynaptic puncta and GLUA2 is, however, unchanged, likely due to the opposing decrease in presynaptic puncta and increase in GLUA2 (VGLUT1-GLUA2 Coloc FC 1.09 ± 0.1; Figure 5M and P; VGLUT2-GLUA2 Coloc FC 1.00 ± 0.08; Figure 5—figure supplement 1L and O).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5M, P and Figure 5—figure supplement 1L, O.

claim: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing identified 22,781 cells in the VGlut2 condition (cKO and WT).
source: This identified 22,781 cells in the VGlut2 condition (cKO and WT) (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq experiment.

claim: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing identified 21,240 cells in the Ip3r2 condition (KO and WT).
source: and 21,240 cells in the Ip3r2 condition (KO and WT) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq experiment.

claim: Initial clustering analysis determined 17 distinct cell populations in both VGlut2 and Ip3r2 models.
source: Initial clustering analysis determined 17 distinct cell populations in both models, with the majority of cells detected clustered within the main glial cell types: astrocytes, microglia, and oligodendrocyte lineage cells (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq clustering analysis.

claim: Unbiased clustering analysis identified four subpopulations of astrocytes in the P14 visual cortex.
source: A second round of unbiased clustering of the astrocyte population identified four groups (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A) in each model and genotype.
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq clustering analysis.

claim: The four astrocyte clusters anatomically correspond to upper (L1–2/3), middle (mid; L2/3–5), deep (L5–6) layer, and white matter (WM) astrocytes.
source: By comparing the genes enriched in each cluster with datasets in the literature, we determined these to anatomically correspond to upper (L1–2/3), middle (mid; L2/3–5), deep (L5–6) layer, and white matter (WM) astrocytes (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A; Batiuk et al., 2020; Bayraktar et al., 2020; Lanjakornsiripan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published datasets and cited literature.

claim: The most robust differences in astrocyte gene expression are between the deep and upper layer astrocytes, with over 700 DEGs and up to sixfold log2 FC in expression level.
source: Pairwise comparisons between each of the clusters using the WT astrocytes of each model as the input cells showed that the most robust differences are between the deep and upper layer astrocytes, with over 700 DEGs and up to sixfold log2 FC in expression level (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2E, Figure 6—source data 1A and B).
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq differential gene expression analysis.

claim: Upper and mid astrocytes are the most similar, with about 200 DEGs and twofold log2 FC maximal difference in mRNA level.
source: On the other hand, upper and mid astrocytes are the most similar, with about 200 DEGs and twofold log2 FC maximal difference in mRNA level (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 2E, Figure 6—source data 1A and B).
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq differential gene expression analysis.

claim: 61 DEGs were identified for the VGlut2 cKO model in astrocytes.
source: We found 61 DEGs for the VGlut2 cKO model and 131 DEGs for the Ip3r2 KO model (Figure 6E–H, Figure 6—source data 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq differential gene expression analysis.

claim: 131 DEGs were identified for the Ip3r2 KO model in astrocytes.
source: We found 61 DEGs for the VGlut2 cKO model and 131 DEGs for the Ip3r2 KO model (Figure 6E–H, Figure 6—source data 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq differential gene expression analysis.

claim: A total of 19 DEGs are common to both the VGlut2 cKO and Ip3r2 KO models.
source: We found a total of 19 DEGs common to both the VGlut2 cKO and Ip3r2 KO models (Figure 6H, Figure 6—source data 1D).
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq differential gene expression analysis.

claim: 79% of common DEGs between VGlut2 cKO and Ip3r2 KO models showed opposing changes.
source: Only one gene was commonly upregulated, and only three genes commonly downregulated (21% of total common DEGs), while the remaining 15 genes showed opposing changes, similar to Gpc4 and Chrdl1 (79% of common DEGs; Figure 6H heatmap).
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq differential gene expression analysis.

claim: 43 common genes were identified between the VGlut2 cKO DEGs and layer-enriched genes (70% of all cKO/WT DEGs).
source: To address this, we compared the list of neuronal or astrocyte activity-regulated genes with the list of layer-enriched genes from the WT (Figure 6I and J, Figure 6—source data 1E) and identified 43 common genes in the VGlut2 cKO model (70% of all cKO/WT DEGs; Figure 6I)
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq analysis comparing DEGs with layer-enriched genes.

claim: 101 common DEGs were identified between the Ip3r2 KO DEGs and layer-enriched genes (77% of all KO/WT DEGs).
source: and 101 common DEGs in the Ip3r2 model (77% of all KO/WT DEGs; Figure 6J).
evidence: This is a result from the snRNAseq analysis comparing DEGs with layer-enriched genes.

claim: 30 DEGs from the VGlut2 cKO dataset were also significantly up- or downregulated at P14 vs. P7 in the bulk RNAseq dataset (52% of all cKO/WT DEGs).
source: This identified 30 DEGs from the VGlut2 cKO dataset (52% of all cKO/WT DEGs, Figure 6—figure supplement 3D)
evidence: This is a result from comparing snRNAseq DEGs with bulk RNAseq developmental changes.

claim: 70% of common DEGs between VGlut2 cKO and developmental changes (P7 vs P14) were regulated in the opposite direction.
source: Comparing the direction of expression changes between normal development and the VGlut2 cKO DEGs, we observed that 70% of common genes were regulated in the opposite direction (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D, middle panel)
evidence: This is a result from comparing snRNAseq DEGs with bulk RNAseq developmental changes.

claim: 57 DEGs from the Ip3r2 KO dataset were commonly identified in the developmental dataset (44% of all KO/WT DEGs).
source: and 57 genes from the Ip3r2 KO dataset (44% of all KO/WT DEGs, Figure 6—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is a result from comparing snRNAseq DEGs with bulk RNAseq developmental changes.

claim: 50% of Ip3r2 KO DEGs displayed the same directionality as during normal development, and the other 50% showed the opposite regulation.
source: On the other hand, Ip3r2 KO data showed 50% of genes displaying the same directionality as during normal development, and the other 50% showing the opposite regulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is a result from comparing snRNAseq DEGs with bulk RNAseq developmental changes.
